### 🔴 PASSAGE 8 — Questions 44–50

> Scenario planning entered corporate practice through an unlikely route. Developed for military contingency analysis, it was adapted in the early 1970s by a planning group at an oil company that had grown uneasy with conventional forecasting. Their concern was not that forecasts were inaccurate — everyone knew that — but that a single forecast, however hedged, produced a single mental model against which all decisions were then made.
>
> The alternative they proposed was to construct several internally coherent narratives about how the future might unfold, each plausible, none designated as most likely. Managers were asked to consider what they would do under each. The purpose was not prediction but preparation: to widen the range of futures that decision-makers had already thought about before they encountered one.
>
> The approach acquired a reputation when the group's scenarios included a sharp rise in oil prices shortly before one occurred. That reputation is somewhat misleading. The value of the exercise did not lie in having guessed correctly; it lay in the fact that managers who had rehearsed the scenario responded faster than those who had not, because the situation was not wholly unfamiliar.
>
> Scenario planning has since been widely adopted, and widely misapplied. The most common failure is to rank the scenarios by probability, which reintroduces exactly the single-forecast thinking the method was designed to displace. A scenario set in which one narrative is treated as the real answer and the others as decoration provides none of the cognitive benefit.

**Q44.** According to the passage, scenario planning was originally developed for:
(a) Oil price forecasting  (b) Military contingency analysis  (c) Academic research  (d) Financial auditing

**Q45.** The planning group's principal concern with conventional forecasting was that:
(a) Forecasts were inaccurate
(b) A single forecast produced a single mental model governing all decisions
(c) Forecasts were too expensive to produce
(d) Managers ignored forecasts entirely

**Q46.** According to the passage, the purpose of constructing multiple scenarios was:
(a) Prediction  (b) Preparation  (c) Regulatory compliance  (d) Cost reduction

**Q47.** The author suggests that the group's reputation for having anticipated the oil price rise is:
(a) Fully deserved  (b) Somewhat misleading  (c) Entirely fabricated  (d) Irrelevant to the method

**Q48.** According to the passage, managers who had rehearsed the scenario responded faster because:
(a) They had more resources
(b) The situation was not wholly unfamiliar
(c) They received earlier warning
(d) They had been given specific instructions

**Q49.** The most common misapplication of scenario planning identified in the passage is:
(a) Constructing too few scenarios
(b) Ranking scenarios by probability
(c) Sharing scenarios with competitors
(d) Updating scenarios too frequently

**Q50.** It can be inferred that the author considers the cognitive benefit of scenario planning to depend on:
(a) The accuracy of the scenarios
(b) Treating multiple scenarios as genuinely plausible rather than designating one as the answer
(c) The seniority of the managers involved
(d) The number of scenarios constructed

## 7. Detailed Solutions

### 🟢 PASSAGE 1 — Solutions 1–5

---

**Q1. Floor-area reduction? → (b) One third or more**

**Locate:** *"…reducing their floor area by **a third or more**."*

This is a detail question — the figure is stated directly.

**Answer: (b) One third or more**

---

**Q2. What loss do teams report? → (b) Informal knowledge transfer**

**Locate:** *"Teams… report a loss of **informal knowledge transfer** — the overheard conversation, the quick question across a desk."*

The dash-clause that follows defines exactly what is meant.

> Options (a), (c) and (d) are all plausible in the real world but appear nowhere in the passage — the classic outside-knowledge trap.

**Answer: (b) Informal knowledge transfer**

---

**Q3. How have organisations responded? → (b) Designating fixed days for teams to attend together**

**Locate:** *"Some organisations have responded by **designating fixed days on which particular teams attend together**, preserving collaboration while retaining the space savings."*

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Reversing the policy entirely | ✗ The passage says savings are **retained** |
| **(b) Fixed days for teams** | **✓ Stated** |
| (c) Higher salaries | ✗ Not mentioned |
| (d) Mandatory five-day attendance | ✗ Contradicts "retaining the space savings" |

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q4. What did the productivity studies find? → (b) Gains in individual tasks, declines in cross-team coordination**

**Locate:** *"Studies… found **gains in individual task completion but declines in cross-team coordination**."*

> **Note the qualifier the passage adds:** "Whether those findings hold under voluntary hybrid arrangements is not yet established." The studies covered *enforced* remote work — a distinction the question preserves by specifying "during enforced remote work".

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q5. The author's stance? → (c) Measured and evidence-focused**

**Evidence for the tone:**

| Passage element | Signal |
|---|---|
| "The financial savings are substantial" | Acknowledges the benefit |
| "Yet the transition has proved less straightforward" | Acknowledges the difficulty |
| "The evidence on productivity remains **mixed**" | Explicit even-handedness |
| "is not yet established" | Refuses to overstate |

The author presents savings, costs and unresolved evidence without endorsing a position.

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Strongly supportive | ✗ The word "Yet" introduces real reservations |
| (b) Strongly opposed | ✗ Savings are called "substantial" |
| **(c) Measured and evidence-focused** | **✓** |
| (d) Indifferent | ✗ The author engages closely with the evidence |

**Answer: (c) Measured and evidence-focused**

---

### 🟢 PASSAGE 2 — Solutions 6–10

---

**Q6. What can young adults not answer questions about? → (b) Compound interest, inflation and risk diversification**

**Locate:** *"…cannot answer basic questions about **compound interest, inflation or risk diversification**."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q7. What do early evaluations show? → (b) Knowledge improves short-term; behavioural effects are smaller and fade**

**Locate:** *"**Knowledge scores improve reliably in the short term**, but the effect on actual financial behaviour… **is smaller and fades over time**."*

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) No improvement of any kind | ✗ Knowledge *does* improve |
| **(b) Knowledge improves; behaviour effect smaller and fades** | **✓ Both halves supported** |
| (c) Behaviour improves more than knowledge | ✗ Reverses the passage |
| (d) Uniformly excellent | ✗ The passage says "modest results" |

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q8. What do the researchers argue? → (b) Simplifying products and improving defaults would achieve more**

**Locate:** *"They contend that **simplifying financial products and improving default options would achieve more than instruction**."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q9. What does the pension example illustrate? → (b) The effectiveness of defaults relative to classroom teaching**

**Locate:** *"Automatically enrolling employees in pension schemes… **raises participation far more effectively than any classroom intervention yet tested**."*

The example appears immediately after the researchers' claim and functions as its evidence.

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q10. Which best captures the structure? → (a) Problem, attempted remedy, alternative view**

**Paragraph summaries:**
```
¶1  →  the PROBLEM (low financial literacy and its consequences)
¶2  →  the REMEDY attempted (school curricula) and its modest results
¶3  →  an ALTERNATIVE VIEW (simplify products, change defaults)
```

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| **(a) Problem, remedy, alternative view** | **✓ Matches all three paragraphs** |
| (b) Two theories and a resolution | ✗ No resolution is offered |
| (c) Chronological history | ✗ No time sequence is developed |
| (d) One argument with three examples | ✗ ¶3 opposes rather than supports ¶2 |

**Answer: (a)**

---

### 🟡 PASSAGE 3 — Solutions 11–16

---

**Q11. How does professional-services automation differ? → (b) Absorbs part of a task rather than a whole task**

**Locate:** *"On a factory floor, a machine typically replaces a whole task… In an audit or advisory practice, software more often **absorbs a portion of a task**, leaving judgement-intensive elements with the professional."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q12. What can software not yet do? → (c) Determine whether an exception is a clerical error, a timing difference, or requires escalation**

**Locate:** *"What it cannot yet do is **decide whether an exception represents a clerical error, a timing difference, or something requiring escalation**."*

> Options (a) and (b) describe what the software **can** do — the sentence immediately before states that it matches millions of transactions and flags exceptions.

**Answer: (c)**

---

**Q13. What happens to the hours saved? → (b) Redeployed toward analysis previously deferred or omitted**

**Locate:** *"The hours saved are not simply removed from the engagement; they are **redeployed toward analysis that was previously deferred or omitted**."*

> **Option (a) is the explicit negation** the passage rules out — "not simply removed from the engagement". Test-setters routinely offer the rejected alternative as a distractor.

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q14. The concern in the final paragraph? → (c) Associates may lack an instinct for normal transaction flows**

**Locate:** *"Removing it risks producing professionals who can evaluate exceptions **without having developed an instinct for the baseline against which exceptions are defined**."*

"The baseline" refers back to "what normal transaction flows look like" in the preceding sentence.

**Answer: (c)**

---

**Q15. The author's view of manual reconciliation? → (b) Tedious but educationally useful**

**Locate:** *"Manual work, **however tedious**, **taught associates what normal transaction flows look like**."*

The concessive phrase "however tedious" grants the drawback; the main clause asserts the value. Both halves are needed.

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Wholly without value | ✗ Directly contradicted |
| **(b) Tedious but educationally useful** | **✓ Both halves supported** |
| (c) Most important part of an audit | ✗ Overstates; not claimed |
| (d) Impossible to automate | ✗ The passage says it *has* been automated |

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q16. Primary purpose? → (b) Explain how automation is reshaping, rather than eliminating, junior work**

**Paragraph summaries:**
```
¶1  →  professional-services automation is PARTIAL, not wholesale
¶2  →  a worked example (reconciliation) showing what remains human
¶3  →  the consequence: junior work CHANGES SHAPE, does not disappear
¶4  →  a training implication of that change
```

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Abandon automation | ✗ Never recommended |
| **(b) Reshaping, not eliminating, junior work** | **✓ Covers all four paragraphs** |
| (c) Compare costs | ✗ Costs are not discussed |
| (d) Software will replace auditors | ✗ Directly contradicted by ¶1 and ¶3 |

**Answer: (b)**

---

### 🟡 PASSAGE 4 — Solutions 17–22

---

**Q17. When is translation performed? → (b) Before consolidation**

**Locate:** *"A subsidiary's results… must be translated into the parent's reporting currency **before consolidation**."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q18. Rupee revenue growth in the example? → (c) 12%**

**Locate:** *"…whose Indian subsidiary **grew revenue by 12% in rupee terms**…"*

**Answer: (c) 12%**

---

**Q19. Growth shown in the consolidated statements? → (a) 2%**

**Locate:** *"The consolidated statements would show **growth of roughly 2%**…"*

**The arithmetic behind it** (worth understanding, though the figure is stated):
$$1.12 \times 0.91 = 1.019 \implies \approx 2\%$$

> **Q18 and Q19 test the same sentence pair** and differ only in *which* figure is asked for. Read the question stem carefully: "in rupee terms" versus "consolidated statements".

**Answer: (a) 2%**

---

**Q20. Constant-currency reporting is: → (c) Not universal, applied with varying methodologies**

**Locate:** *"The practice is **not universal**, and where it is adopted **the methodology varies**."*

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Legally mandatory | ✗ Never stated |
| (b) Universal with a standard methodology | ✗ Directly contradicted |
| **(c) Not universal, methodologies vary** | **✓** |
| (d) Prohibited | ✗ Contradicted — many groups present it |

**Answer: (c)**

---

**Q21. The author's view of translated figures? → (b) Legitimate answers to a legitimate question, but easily misread**

**Locate:** *"**None of this makes translated figures wrong.** Consolidated statements answer **a legitimate question**… The difficulty arises only when that answer is **mistaken for a different one**."*

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Fundamentally misleading | ✗ Explicitly denied — "none of this makes them wrong" |
| **(b) Legitimate but easily misread** | **✓ Both halves stated** |
| (c) Superior in all cases | ✗ Not claimed |
| (d) Relevant only to analysts | ✗ Not stated |

> **The final paragraph exists to prevent exactly the misreading in option (a).** When a passage ends with a qualifying paragraph, that paragraph almost always carries a question.

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q22. Two companies reporting constant-currency growth may: → (b) Be applying materially different assumptions**

**Locate:** *"Two companies reporting constant-currency growth may be applying **materially different assumptions** about which rate to hold constant."*

**Answer: (b)**

### 🔴 PASSAGE 5 — Solutions 23–28

---

**Q23. What did the munitions study show? → (b) Reducing from ~70 to ~50 hours left output essentially unchanged**

**Locate:** *"…reducing the working week from around seventy hours to around fifty **left total output essentially unchanged**."*

> **Note the precision required.** Option (a) says output *rose* — the passage says "unchanged". Option (d) states the opposite of the passage's whole argument.

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q24. Why does the accuracy penalty matter more? → (b) Errors must be found and corrected, often by someone else at greater cost**

**Locate:** *"…because **errors made late in a long day must be found and corrected — often by someone else, and often at greater cost than the original task**."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q25. Why does the assumption persist? → (b) Organisational measurement difficulties**

**Locate:** *"…the reasons are **largely organisational rather than empirical**. Hours are visible and easily measured; output quality frequently is not."*

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Empirical evidence supporting it | ✗ Explicitly ruled out — "rather than empirical" |
| **(b) Organisational measurement difficulties** | **✓** |
| (c) Employee preference | ✗ Not mentioned |
| (d) Legal requirements | ✗ Not mentioned |

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q26. Time spent becomes a proxy for: → (b) Effort**

**Locate:** *"…effort becomes a proxy for contribution, and **time spent becomes a proxy for effort**."*

> **Read the chain carefully.** There are two proxies in one sentence: effort → contribution, and time → **effort**. The question asks about *time spent*, so the answer is **effort**, not contribution.

**Answer: (b) Effort**

---

**Q27. The correct sequence? → (b) Define good output first, then address the schedule**

**Locate:** *"Organisations that have succeeded… have generally done so by **first establishing what good output looks like, and only then addressing the schedule**. Attempts to reverse that order have tended to fail."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q28. The author's attitude to the long-hours assumption? → (b) Sceptical and analytical**

**Evidence:**

| Passage element | Signal |
|---|---|
| "has proved remarkably durable, **despite evidence**… pointing the other way" | Scepticism |
| "The mechanism is **not mysterious**" | Analytical, matter-of-fact |
| "the reasons are largely organisational rather than empirical" | Diagnostic |
| "requires **better measurement rather than exhortation**" | Constructive, not outraged |

The author rejects the assumption and explains why it survives — sceptical about the belief, analytical in approach.

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Sympathetic | ✗ The whole passage argues against it |
| **(b) Sceptical and analytical** | **✓** |
| (c) Neutral and uncommitted | ✗ The author clearly takes a position |
| (d) Outraged | ✗ The register is measured throughout |

**Answer: (b) Sceptical and analytical**

### 🔴 PASSAGE 6 — TRUE / FALSE / CANNOT SAY: Solutions 29–36

---

**Q29. "Revenue of ₹1,240 crore for 2023–24." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"Meridian Logistics reported revenue of **₹1,240 crore** for the financial year **2023–24**."*

Stated verbatim.

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q30. "Revenue in 2022–23 was higher than in 2023–24." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"…an **increase of 18%** over the previous year."*

An increase means the previous year's revenue was **lower**, not higher. The statement asserts the opposite.

**Answer: FALSE**

> **This is a contradiction, not a gap.** The passage does not state the 2022–23 figure explicitly, but "an increase of 18%" logically requires the earlier year to be smaller — so the verdict is False, not Cannot Say.

---

**Q31. "The warehousing division expanded floor area by 40%." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"…the company's warehousing division, which **expanded its floor area by 40%**…"*

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q32. "Meridian acquired three regional operators." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"…following the **acquisition of three regional operators** in the second quarter."*

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q33. "The driver shortage affects only Meridian Logistics." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"…constrained by driver shortages that the company describes as an **industry-wide problem**."*

"Industry-wide" directly contradicts "only Meridian".

**Answer: FALSE**

---

**Q34. "Operating margin increased during the year." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"Operating margin **fell** from 11.2% to 9.8%…"*

A direct contradiction.

**Answer: FALSE**

---

**Q35. "Meridian is the largest logistics company in India." → CANNOT SAY**

The passage gives Meridian's revenue, divisions, margin and dividend policy. It says **nothing** about competitors or market position.

> **This is the archetypal Cannot Say.** The statement is neither supported nor contradicted — the passage simply does not address the subject. Do not reason from the size of the revenue figure; that is outside knowledge.

**Answer: CANNOT SAY**

---

**Q36. "The company declared a dividend for 2023–24." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"**No dividend was declared** for the year."*

**Answer: FALSE**

---

**Summary of Passage 6:**

| Q | Statement | Verdict | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| 29 | Revenue ₹1,240 crore | **TRUE** | Stated |
| 30 | Prior year higher | **FALSE** | "increase of 18%" |
| 31 | Floor area +40% | **TRUE** | Stated |
| 32 | Three acquisitions | **TRUE** | Stated |
| 33 | Shortage affects only Meridian | **FALSE** | "industry-wide" |
| 34 | Margin increased | **FALSE** | "fell from 11.2% to 9.8%" |
| 35 | Largest in India | **CANNOT SAY** | Not addressed |
| 36 | Dividend declared | **FALSE** | "No dividend was declared" |

### 🔴 PASSAGE 7 — TRUE / FALSE / CANNOT SAY: Solutions 37–43

---

**Q37. "The review examined 180 engagements." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"A recent review… examined **180 engagements** conducted between 2021 and 2023."*

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q38. "Fully remote engagements took 14% longer on average." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"…engagements performed **entirely remotely** took, on average, **14% longer** than comparable on-site engagements…"*

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q39. "The time difference grew larger over the period." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"…though the difference **narrowed considerably** in the later part of the period."*

"Narrowed" is the direct opposite of "grew larger".

**Answer: FALSE**

---

**Q40. "Clients with mature document-management systems showed no significant time penalty." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"Where clients had mature document-management systems, remote engagements showed **no significant time penalty**."*

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q41. "The review concluded that remote audits are lower in quality." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"The reviewers **made no assessment of audit quality**, noting that the available data did not permit a reliable comparison."*

The statement asserts a conclusion the review explicitly declined to reach. Since the passage directly denies that any such conclusion was drawn, this is a **contradiction**.

**Answer: FALSE**

> **Distinguish this from Cannot Say.** If the passage had simply not mentioned quality, the answer would be Cannot Say. But it states affirmatively that **no assessment was made**, which contradicts the claim that a conclusion was reached.

---

**Q42. "The reviewers recommended further work on audit quality." → TRUE**

**Locate:** *"They recommended that **future work address this gap**."*

"This gap" refers to the quality assessment they could not make.

**Answer: TRUE**

---

**Q43. "All 180 engagements were conducted remotely." → FALSE**

**Locate:** *"…engagements performed entirely remotely took… longer than **comparable on-site engagements**."*

The comparison requires that **some** of the engagements were on-site. If all 180 had been remote, there would have been no on-site group to compare against.

**Answer: FALSE**

> **This one requires a small inference**, but the inference is *necessary*: a comparison between remote and on-site engagements presupposes that both existed within the study.

---

**Summary of Passage 7:**

| Q | Statement | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 37 | 180 engagements examined | **TRUE** |
| 38 | 14% longer on average | **TRUE** |
| 39 | Difference grew larger | **FALSE** |
| 40 | Mature systems: no penalty | **TRUE** |
| 41 | Concluded remote audits lower quality | **FALSE** |
| 42 | Recommended further work on quality | **TRUE** |
| 43 | All 180 were remote | **FALSE** |

### 🔴 PASSAGE 8 — Solutions 44–50

---

**Q44. Scenario planning was originally developed for: → (b) Military contingency analysis**

**Locate:** *"Developed for **military contingency analysis**, it was adapted in the early 1970s by a planning group at an oil company…"*

> The oil company **adapted** it; it did not develop it. Option (a) reverses the sequence.

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q45. The group's principal concern with forecasting? → (b) A single forecast produced a single mental model**

**Locate:** *"Their concern was **not that forecasts were inaccurate — everyone knew that** — but that a single forecast, however hedged, **produced a single mental model against which all decisions were then made**."*

> **The "not X but Y" construction is doing decisive work here.** Option (a) is precisely what the passage rules out. Whenever you see "not… but…", expect the rejected half to appear as a distractor.

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q46. The purpose of multiple scenarios? → (b) Preparation**

**Locate:** *"The purpose was **not prediction but preparation**: to widen the range of futures that decision-makers had already thought about…"*

**Answer: (b) Preparation**

---

**Q47. The group's reputation for anticipating the oil price rise is: → (b) Somewhat misleading**

**Locate:** *"That reputation is **somewhat misleading**. The value of the exercise did not lie in having guessed correctly…"*

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Fully deserved | ✗ Contradicted |
| **(b) Somewhat misleading** | **✓ Stated verbatim** |
| (c) Entirely fabricated | ✗ Too strong — the scenarios *did* include the rise |
| (d) Irrelevant to the method | ✗ The author uses it to make a point about the method |

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q48. Why did rehearsed managers respond faster? → (b) The situation was not wholly unfamiliar**

**Locate:** *"…managers who had rehearsed the scenario responded faster than those who had not, **because the situation was not wholly unfamiliar**."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q49. The most common misapplication? → (b) Ranking scenarios by probability**

**Locate:** *"The most common failure is to **rank the scenarios by probability**, which reintroduces exactly the single-forecast thinking the method was designed to displace."*

**Answer: (b)**

---

**Q50. The cognitive benefit depends on: → (b) Treating multiple scenarios as genuinely plausible rather than designating one as the answer**

**Locate:** *"A scenario set in which **one narrative is treated as the real answer and the others as decoration provides none of the cognitive benefit**."*

**Step 1 — Read the negative formulation.**
The passage states the condition under which the benefit is **lost**: when one scenario is privileged.

**Step 2 — Invert it.**
The benefit is therefore preserved when all scenarios are treated as genuinely plausible — which is option (b).

| Option | Assessment |
|---|---|
| (a) Accuracy of the scenarios | ✗ Explicitly denied in ¶3 — "did not lie in having guessed correctly" |
| **(b) Treating multiple scenarios as genuinely plausible** | **✓** |
| (c) Seniority of managers | ✗ Not mentioned |
| (d) Number of scenarios | ✗ Not the criterion the passage identifies |

**Answer: (b)**

> **A negative statement inverts into a positive inference.** "X provides none of the benefit" implies the benefit requires not-X. This is a common and legitimate one-step inference — and a frequent basis for the hardest RC questions.

## 8. Quick Revision Sheet

> **One page. Read 48 hours after study, and again the night before the test.**

### ⭐ The method

```
1.  Skim the QUESTIONS first (not the options)      —  20 s
2.  Read the passage with those questions in mind   —  90 s
3.  Answer, returning to the text for details       — 110 s
                                              TOTAL ≈ 4 min per 5-Q passage

Mark as you read:
    ¶1 ¶2 ¶3  →  one-word summary each
    CIRCLE     →  however · but · therefore · although
    UNDERLINE  →  numbers · dates · proper nouns
```

### The four question types

```
DETAIL      "According to the passage…"   →  LOCATE the exact line
INFERENCE   "It can be inferred…"         →  ONE step beyond the text
MAIN IDEA   "The primary purpose…"        →  must cover the WHOLE passage
TONE        "The author's tone is…"       →  look at adjectives and qualifiers
```

### The evidence rule

```
Every correct answer must be traceable to specific words in the passage.
If you cannot point to the line, the option is wrong —
however true it may be in the real world.
```

### How wrong options are built

```
TOO EXTREME        all · never · only · proves · completely
OUTSIDE KNOWLEDGE  true in the world, absent from the passage
PARTIALLY CORRECT  one clause supported, another not
WRONG SCOPE        describes one ¶ when the whole passage is asked about
FAMILIAR WORDING   reuses a distinctive phrase but changes the claim
REJECTED HALF      the "not X but Y" construction — X is offered as a distractor
```

### Passage structures

```
A  CLAIM → EVIDENCE → IMPLICATION      main idea in ¶1
B  PROBLEM → CAUSE → REMEDY            main idea spans the passage
C  VIEW A → VIEW B → AUTHOR'S VIEW     main idea in the last ¶
D  PAST → PRESENT → OUTLOOK            main idea is the trajectory

"HOWEVER" is the most important word in any passage —
the sentence after it usually carries what is being tested.
```

### ⭐ TRUE / FALSE / CANNOT SAY

```
TRUE        →  the passage says it, or logically requires it
FALSE       →  the passage says the opposite, or rules it out
CANNOT SAY  →  the passage does not address it

DECISION PROCEDURE
    1.  Does the passage say / require this?      YES → TRUE
    2.  Does the passage contradict / rule out?   YES → FALSE
    3.  Otherwise                                     → CANNOT SAY

"CANNOT SAY" IS CORRECT MORE OFTEN THAN CANDIDATES EXPECT
    — typically 3 or 4 out of 8 statements.
    If you are marking almost everything True or False,
    you are importing outside knowledge.

THE QUANTIFIER LADDER
    all/every  >  most  >  many  >  some  >  a few  >  may/might

    Passage "all"  → statement "some"  →  TRUE      (downgrading is safe)
    Passage "some" → statement "all"   →  CANNOT SAY (upgrading is not)

FALSE vs CANNOT SAY
    "Revenue rose 12%" → "Revenue fell"     →  FALSE   (contradiction)
    "Revenue rose 12%" → "Profit rose"      →  CANNOT SAY (not addressed)
    "No assessment was made" → "They concluded X"  →  FALSE (denied)
```

### Tone vocabulary

```
NEUTRAL     reports without evaluation
ANALYTICAL  weighs evidence; "although", "on balance"
CRITICAL    flawed · inadequate · misguided
CAUTIOUS    may · might · suggests · appears
BALANCED    presents both benefits and difficulties

Most professional passages are NEUTRAL, ANALYTICAL or BALANCED.
Extreme options — scathing, euphoric, outraged — are almost always wrong.
```

---

## 9. Common Mistakes

| # | Mistake | Example | Correction |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Reading the passage before the questions** | Studying it in full first | Skim the questions in 20 seconds first |
| 2 | **Outside knowledge used** | "Parrots are birds, so…" | Use only what the passage states |
| 3 | **Extreme option accepted** | "exempt from **all** regulation" | The passage said "most direct pressure" |
| 4 | **Inference over-extended** | "Costs rose ⇒ will make a loss" | One step only: "margins narrowed" |
| 5 | **Main idea taken from one paragraph** | Choosing a ¶2 summary | It must cover the whole passage |
| 6 | **Familiar phrasing trusted** | An option reusing a distinctive phrase | Check whether the *claim* matches |
| 7 | **The rejected half chosen** | "not X but Y" ⇒ selecting X | The passage explicitly denies X |
| 8 | **Cannot Say under-used** | Marking everything True or False | 3–4 of 8 are typically Cannot Say |
| 9 | **Cannot Say over-used** | Marking a contradiction as Cannot Say | If the passage denies it, it is FALSE |
| 10 | **Quantifier upgraded** | "some" read as "all" | Downgrade is safe; upgrade is not |
| 11 | **Adjacent figure taken** | "nearly all" (intending) read as "able to now" | Match the figure to the right subject |
| 12 | **Extreme tone selected** | "outraged" for a measured passage | Prefer neutral / analytical / balanced |
| 13 | **Passage re-read in full** | Reading it twice | Return to specific lines only |
| 14 | **Blank left** | Skipping a hard inference question | No negative marking — always answer |

---

## Practice Answer Key

| Q | Ans | Q | Ans | Q | Ans | Q | Ans | Q | Ans |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | b | 11 | b | 21 | b | 31 | TRUE | 41 | FALSE |
| 2 | b | 12 | c | 22 | b | 32 | TRUE | 42 | TRUE |
| 3 | b | 13 | b | 23 | b | 33 | FALSE | 43 | FALSE |
| 4 | b | 14 | c | 24 | b | 34 | FALSE | 44 | b |
| 5 | c | 15 | b | 25 | b | 35 | CANNOT SAY | 45 | b |
| 6 | b | 16 | b | 26 | b | 36 | FALSE | 46 | b |
| 7 | b | 17 | b | 27 | b | 37 | TRUE | 47 | b |
| 8 | b | 18 | c | 28 | b | 38 | TRUE | 48 | b |
| 9 | b | 19 | a | 29 | TRUE | 39 | FALSE | 49 | b |
| 10 | a | 20 | c | 30 | FALSE | 40 | TRUE | 50 | b |

**Scoring guide:** 42+/50 → strong. 32–41 → solid; focus on the True/False/Cannot Say sets (Passages 6 and 7) — the discipline there transfers to every other RC question. Below 32 → the usual cause is importing outside knowledge. Redo the set with one rule: **point to the line** before selecting any answer.

> **Timing benchmark:** a 5-question passage should take **4 minutes**. If you are exceeding 6 minutes, you are reading the passage too carefully on the first pass. Skim, then hunt.
